'''''Dianella tasmanica''''', commonly known as the '''Tasman flax-lily''' or '''Tasmanian flax-lily''',<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.abc.net.au/gardening/stories/s1164543.htm |title=Gardening Australia - Fact Sheet: Dividing Australian Tufties |website=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]] |access-date=2010-11-11 |archive-date=2010-05-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100515111244/http://www.abc.net.au/gardening/stories/s1164543.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{APNI | name = Dianella tasmanica | id = 46692}}</ref> is a herbaceous strappy perennial herb of the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Asphodelaceae]], subfamily [[Hemerocallidoideae]], found in southeastern Australia including Tasmania. Its leaves are up to {{convert|80|cm|abbr=off|sigfig=1}} in length, and the flower stem is up to {{convert|1.5|m|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name="food">{{cite book|title=Wild food plants of Australia|author=Tim Low|publisher= HarperCollins|edition=2nd|date=31 July 1991|isbn=978-0207169304}}</ref> Blue flowers in spring and summer are followed by violet berries. It adapts readily to cultivation and is commonly seen in Australian gardens. Unlike other ''[[Dianella (plant)|Dianella]]'' species, its fruits are toxic.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ozbreed.com.au/plant-ranges/dianellas/|title = Dianella Plants: Caerulea, Tasmanica, Revouta & Purina|website=Ozbreed.com.au}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Dianella tasmanica'' was first described in 1858 by eminent English botanist and explorer [[Joseph Dalton Hooker]].<ref name=hooker>Hooker, J.D. (1858), [https://biodiversitylibrary.org/page/28467640 The botany of the Antarctic voyage of H.M. discovery ships Erebus and Terror. III. Flora Tasmaniae 2(6): 57, t. CXXXIII.]</ref> The genus name is derived from the Roman goddess [[Diana (mythology)|Diana]], with a diminutive suffix -''ella''.<ref name=Enc/>

==Description==
''Dianella tasmanica'' is a strappy herbaceous plant which grows to 0.5–2 metres (1–7 ft) high and wide, with a thick spreading rhizome under the ground. The green linear keeled leaves have finely toothed margins, and may reach 1 m (40 in) in length and 1.5–4 cm wide. The small (1.5 cm diameter) blue flowers bloom in spring and summer (August to February), and are followed by small roughly oval or globular violet berries which range from about 1.2 cm (0.5 in) in diameter.<ref name=Enc>{{cite book | last1=Elliot | first1=Rodger W. | last2=Jones | first2=David L. | last3=Blake | first3=Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Volume 3|year=1984|page=260 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-167-2}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Found southwards from [[Dorrigo, New South Wales|Dorrigo]] in New South Wales,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Dianella~tasmanica|title=Dianella tasmanica Hook.f.|last=Wilson|first=K. L.|work=PlantNET - NSW Flora Online|publisher= Royal Botanic Gardens & Domain Trust, Sydney |access-date=2009-10-11}}</ref>  and into Victoria and Tasmania, ''Dianella tasmanica'' grows singly or in clumps in shady spots in wet forests.<ref name=Enc/>

==Cultivation==
''Dianella tasmanica'' is a hardy plant which has been cultivated in gardens and as a pot plant for many years in Australia, preferring shade and regular moisture.<ref name=Enc/> It can also be grown as an indoor plant, in a brightly lit space.<ref>{{cite book |title=Australian Native Plants for Indoors |last=Ratcliffe |first=David & Patricia|year=1987 |publisher=Little Hills Press |location=Crows Nest, NSW |isbn=0-949773-49-2 |page=44}}</ref> A form with variegated leaves known as "Rainbow" is in cultivation, as well as a compact form "Little Devil", and a salt-tolerant form with red-tinged leaves.<ref name="Davis 2009">{{cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2009/dianella-tasmanica.html|title=Dianella tasmanica |last=Davis |first=Lesleigh Lougheed|date=2009|work=Growing Native Plants|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|access-date=2009-10-11|location=Canberra, ACT}}</ref>

== Uses ==
The fruits of ''Dianella tasmanica'' are toxic to an unknown degree and should not be eaten. They are markedly larger than the fruits of other ''Dianella'' species, and produce an irritating tingling sensation in the mouth when consumed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dianella Plants: Caerulea, Tasmanica, Revouta & Purina |url=https://www.ozbreed.com.au/plant-ranges/dianellas/ |access-date=2022-06-16 |website=Ozbreed Plants |language=en-AU}}</ref> The fruits have reportedly been used by [[Aboriginal Australians|Aboriginal peoples]] to dye baskets, and the leaves may be used for weaving.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Australian National Botanic Gardens |first=Parks Australia |title=Dianella tasmanica - Growing Native Plants |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2009/dianella-tasmanica.html |access-date=2022-06-16 |website=www.anbg.gov.au |language=en}}</ref>
